College Class Methods.—Although, as the catalog rule indicates, the basic classroom method even in collegiate courses was that of orally testing the students' grasp of the assigned material in the textbook, the procedure as actually practiced was more that of classroom discussion than of mechanical question and answer. The students, being older and often highly intelligent, were capable of owners or contributing to the discussion, and questions could come from the students as well as the professor. This procedure naturally led to informal lecturing or exposition on the part of the professor.

    In science courses requiring laboratory demonstrations, students were appointed or chosen, it would seem, to go to the laboratory and make preparations for the experiment for the day's work. One of the College laboratories had students performed and explained the experiment to the class, as sufficient equipment may not have been to permit each student to perform his own experiment.

Expansion of the Plant.

    The Buildings.—By the time of the incorporation of the College, as has been noted in Chapter III, the College plant consisted of a number of frame buildings, including one very large room and one of smaller dimensions and a two-story frame building with dormitory space. The buildings, having plenty of window and door space and good ventilation, were of log construction, which were provided as bachelor's halls for young men who did not wish to room in town, living in them and doing their own housekeeping and cooking. These "back halls" as students called them, were considered the college campus on the east.

    As the College grew in size and notoriety, it was the custom to erect a temporary outdoor stage against the wall of a building and to provide temporary bench seats for the annual "exhibition" which marked the close of the year's work.
